title: The Great Water Mystery
markdown:
On a shimmering morning, when the sun had already climbed high and painted the leaves gold, Ivo the iguana and Tika the gecko found themselves parched. They had searched for damp spots, but the sun had baked those dry. Their tongues felt like dry leaves.

“We need a drink, Ivo,” Tika said, tiny toes tapping a restless rhythm on a sun-baked stone. Her bright eyes scanned the forest floor for a puddle or a dripping leaf.

Ivo, the thoughtful planner, nodded. His long tail gave a gentle swish. “Thirst is a stern visitor. I have prepared two bowls of our freshest water. One rests by the old oak’s roots, where the shade is deep and the air is cool and still. The other sits upon the flat, sun-warmed rock near the berry bushes, the bright place you like.” He pointed with his snout, movements slow. “We shall watch, and see which spot keeps our water best.”

They filled the bowls from a shaded spring, water cool and clear, each brim even with the other. Tika counted the drips as they poured, to be fair. She skittered to the sunny rock, set her bowl with care, and stretched in the warmth. “This spot is so bright and cheerful.” Ivo took his bowl to the oak’s roots, ancient branches reaching like arms, and pressed it into a dimple of moss so it would not tip. “And this spot is calm and quiet,” he said, settling with a soft rustle of scales.

They waited. Waiting, Ivo said, was part of watching. A beetle crossed Tika’s rock and did not drink. A wren sang once and left. The sun climbed. Shadows stretched and shrank. A breeze began to whisper through the leaves. It tickled Tika as she peered into her bowl. The water, which had been perfectly full, seemed to have shrunk. A little ripple ran, then another. The sun-warmed surface shimmered, and a faint, almost silent hiss rose as the breeze nudged it.

“Ivo. My water is much lower than when we started. Look.”

Ivo ambled over, tail dragging a faint trail on moss. He looked into Tika’s bowl, then into his own, nestled in the oak’s cool dark. “Mine is still quite full. The sun is warm on your rock, and the breeze plays there. My bowl is shaded, and the air is still.”

Tika dipped a toe. “It is warm.” She pulled back, then darted to Ivo’s bowl. “And yours is still cool.” She looked from rock to roots. A small understanding moved through her. The warmth and the wind seemed to be carrying the water away, as if tiny invisible pieces were floating into the sky.

“Let’s try something else.” They found a small smooth stone and set it in Tika’s remaining water. The level rose a little, making space. “See? The water is still here when we add a stone. It does not vanish into nothing. But when it gets warm and the air moves…” She tapped her foot. A puff of air lifted a speck of dust. She watched the surface, wondering.

They tried a more careful watch. They took a third, smaller bowl and set it in a deep cool hollow, far from direct sun, sheltered from every puff of wind by thick bushes and mossy rocks. They filled it from the spring until the surface matched the others as nearly as their eyes could tell. Then they sat: Ivo under his oak, Tika darting around the hollow and back to the rock, comparing, frowning, hoping.

The afternoon was long. A cloud passed and Tika thought her rock-bowl might be saved, but the cloud was thin and the breeze did not stop. Ivo dozed without quite sleeping, one eye on his own still water.

By the time the light leaned toward orange and pink, they checked all three. The hollow bowl was almost as full as at the start, barely a drop gone. The oak bowl was a little lower—even shade is not entirely still—but it held plenty. Tika’s bowl on the sunny rock was nearly empty. Only a tiny sad puddle remained.

Ivo rumbled, quiet wonder in it. “The sun’s warmth made the water want to rise. The moving air helped it float away.”

“So the water doesn’t disappear forever?” Tika said. “It floats up into the air?”

“It turns into vapour,” Ivo said. “A kind of gas you cannot easily see. When warmth and moving air are right, liquid water becomes vapour and dances into the sky. That is why the hot, breezy rock emptied so quickly. Too lively a place for water to rest. People call this evaporation. It is why a puddle on a path shrinks on a sunny, windy day, and why clothes on a line dry.”

Tika’s eyes sparkled. To keep water safe on warm days, they would need shade and stillness, where a drink could wait. She found herself wondering, “What else in the world floats away like that?” Dew on a quiet morning, she thought, and steam above a kettle, and a great many other secrets still sitting in plain light, waiting for two thirsty friends to watch.
